entities.name: Narayan Hemchandra
entities.intro: An eccentric Gujarati writer and translator, oddly dressed, who arrived in London wanting to learn English.

entities.name: Cardinal Manning
entities.intro: Catholic Archbishop of Westminster, famous for helping settle the 1889 London dock strike.

entities.name: Paris
entities.intro: Gandhi visited the 1890 Exposition Universelle here.

entities.name: Leo Tolstoy
entities.intro: Russian novelist and religious thinker.

entities.name: Frederick Pincutt
entities.intro: Conservative lawyer in London known for his kindness to Indian students.

entities.name: Sir Pherozeshah Mehta
entities.intro: Bombay's leading barrister and political boss, said to roar 'like a lion' in court.

entities.name: Raychandbhai (Shrimad Rajchandra)
entities.intro: Jain poet, jeweller and spiritual seeker, about 25 years old, related to Dr. Mehta by marriage. Famous for his feats of memory.

entities.name: Revashankar Jagjivan
entities.intro: Dr. Mehta's brother, a Bombay jeweller, who became a lifelong friend of Gandhi.

entities.name: John Ruskin
entities.intro: English critic and social thinker.

entities.name: Ravishankar (the cook)
entities.intro: Gandhi's cheerful, unwashed Brahman cook in Bombay.

entities.name: Virchand Gandhi
entities.intro: A Bombay friend reading for the solicitor's exam.

entities.name: Mamibai
entities.intro: A client in a small-causes case, Gandhi's first.

entities.name: The Political Agent
entities.intro: The British officer overseeing Kathiawad's states. Gandhi had met him in England.

entities.name: Manilal Gandhi
entities.intro: Gandhi's second son, born 1892 after Gandhi's return from England.

entities.name: Abdul Karim Jhaveri
entities.intro: Partner in Dada Abdulla and Co. in Porbandar.

entities.name: Dada Abdulla Sheth
entities.intro: Head of Dada Abdulla & Co. in Durban, one of the largest Indian firms in South Africa. Barely literate but shrewd, proud of Islam, and suspicious by nature.

entities.name: Natal & Durban
entities.intro: British colony on South Africa's east coast, with a large Indian population of indentured labourers and merchants. Durban is its port.

entities.name: South Africa
entities.intro: A patchwork of British colonies (Natal, Cape) and Boer republics (Transvaal, Orange Free State).

entities.name: East African ports
entities.intro: Ports of call on the voyage from Bombay to Natal.

entities.name: The ship's Captain
entities.intro: Captain of the ship that took Gandhi to South Africa in 1893.

entities.name: Racial discrimination
entities.intro: How the colonial order treats Indians and other non-whites.

entities.name: Indians in South Africa
entities.intro: South Africa's Indian community: Muslim merchants who called themselves 'Arabs', Hindu and Parsi clerks, and a large majority of indentured Tamil, Telugu and North Indian labourers.

entities.name: Islam
entities.intro: Gandhi's understanding of Islam.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is in his last year in London: frugal, vegetarian, still shy, and newly interested in religion.
chapters.summary: Gandhi befriends Narayan Hemchandra, a scruffy, grammar-free Gujarati author with boundless ambition. They swap vegetarian cooking, and Gandhi interprets when Hemchandra calls on Cardinal Manning to thank him for his work in the dock strike. Hemchandra walks London in a dhoti, goes on to Paris, and travels to America on deck.

updates.gandhi: Lives on 17s a week and cooks for himself. Teaches English to Hemchandra and acts as his interpreter with Cardinal Manning.
updates.hemchandra: Becomes Gandhi's daily companion. Visits Cardinal Manning in his usual shabby clothes, telling Gandhi that 'great men never look at a person's exterior'. Later goes to Paris and then America, where he is prosecuted for wearing a dhoti.
updates.manning: Receives Gandhi and Hemchandra briefly and blesses them.
updates.simplicity: Hemchandra's carefree poverty and third-class travel make a strong impression on Gandhi.

status.hemchandra: Left London for Paris and America

chapters.situation: Gandhi is nearing the end of his London studies and has just said goodbye to his eccentric friend Hemchandra.
chapters.summary: Gandhi spends a frugal week in Paris for the 1890 Exhibition, staying at a vegetarian restaurant. He climbs the Eiffel Tower and spends seven shillings on lunch up it. The devotion he sees in Notre Dame convinces him that worship before images is not mere superstition. He agrees with Tolstoy that the Tower is a toy.

updates.gandhi: Visits the Paris Exhibition on foot and on a budget; is deeply moved by Paris's cathedrals.
updates.tolstoy: First mention: his view that the Eiffel Tower is a monument to folly, a product of a tobacco-clouded mind.
updates.paris: Seven days at the 1890 Exhibition, the Eiffel Tower and Notre Dame.
updates.religion: Watching worshippers kneel before the Virgin, Gandhi senses they worship the divinity behind the stone and that this adds to God's glory.
updates.christianity: Notre Dame's peace and devotion impress him.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has toured Paris and returns to London for the last stretch of his law studies.
chapters.summary: Bar students qualify largely by 'eating dinners' at their Inn; Gandhi abstains from wine and is popular in drinking foursomes. He reads all the textbooks properly, including Roman Law in Latin, which later helps him with South Africa's Roman-Dutch law. He is called to the bar on 10 June 1891, enrolls in the High Court on the 11th, and sails home on the 12th, still feeling unqualified to practise.

updates.gandhi: Called to the bar on 10 June 1891 and sails for India on the 12th. Has studied hard but feels helpless about actually practising.
updates.law: English bar exams are easy; Gandhi studies every text anyway. Roman law in Latin will later help him in South Africa.
updates.diet: Gandhi and a Parsi student successfully apply for the benchers' vegetarian courses at Inn dinners.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has been called to the bar but has learned no Indian law and does not know how to practise.
chapters.summary: Gandhi is too timid to ask the great Dadabhai Naoroji for advice. The kindly Conservative Frederick Pincutt tells him that honesty and industry are enough to make an ordinary lawyer, and tells him to read Indian history and books on reading character from faces. Gandhi sails home on the S.S. Assam with 'a little leaven of hope'.

updates.gandhi: Leaves England afraid he cannot earn a living at the bar, but somewhat reassured by Pincutt.
updates.dadabhai: Gandhi attends his talks from a corner. Dadabhai offers advice anytime, but Gandhi is too shy to take it up.
updates.pincutt: Laughs away Gandhi's pessimism: 'Do you think that everyone must be a Pherozeshah Mehta?' Recommends reading Indian history.
updates.pherozeshah: Mentioned as the brilliant Bombay barrister Gandhi fears he can never equal.
updates.law: Gandhi knows no Hindu or Muslim law and cannot draft a plaint.

status.gandhi: Barrister returning to India, unsure of himself

chapters.situation: Gandhi, newly a barrister, has just landed in Bombay full of doubts about practising law, with his caste dispute still unresolved.
chapters.summary: His brother meets him and tells him their mother died while he was in England; the news had been kept from him. Gandhi grieves without outward display. At Dr. Mehta's he meets the young jeweller-poet Raychandbhai, whose memory, purity and passion for seeing God make him Gandhi's spiritual refuge, though never his guru. Gandhi names Raychandbhai, Tolstoy and Ruskin as the three moderns who most shaped him.

updates.gandhi: Learns of his mother's death on landing; his grief is greater than for his father. Finds a spiritual guide in Raychandbhai.
updates.putlibai: Died while Gandhi was in England; his brother hid the news until he was home.
updates.laxmidas: Meets him at the dock and hides their mother's death until he is back in India.
updates.pjmehta: Puts Gandhi up in Bombay; the friendship becomes a lifelong bond between their families.
updates.raychand: Met at Dr. Mehta's. A jeweller dealing in huge sums who reads scripture between deals. He becomes Gandhi's 'refuge' in spiritual crises, though Gandhi cannot call him guru.
updates.revashankar: Introduced by Dr. Mehta; the start of a lifelong friendship.
updates.tolstoy: Named as one of the three moderns who most shaped Gandhi, through 'The Kingdom of God Is Within You'.
updates.ruskin: Named as one of the three moderns who most shaped Gandhi, through 'Unto This Last'.
updates.religion: Gandhi believes in the Hindu ideal of a guru, but the 'throne remains vacant'.

status.putlibai: Died while Gandhi was in England

chapters.situation: Back in India, Gandhi has lost his mother and found a mentor in Raychandbhai. He now has to earn a living.
chapters.summary: His brother performs a purification bath and caste dinner, which satisfies one faction of the caste. Gandhi quietly accepts the other faction's ban rather than fight it. He remains jealous of Kasturbai and once sends her to her father's house. He Europeanizes the household with oatmeal, cocoa and European dress, and drives up expenses. He tries Bombay, where he runs a household with the unwashed Brahman cook Ravishankar.

updates.gandhi: Back in Rajkot and Bombay, Europeanizing the household and teaching the family children exercise. Still jealous and unkind to his wife. Moves to Bombay to try for briefs.
updates.kasturba: Sent away to her father's house once by her jealous husband and taken back only after being made 'thoroughly miserable'.
updates.laxmidas: Has built the household up in expectation of his brother's success. Arranges the purification bath at Nasik and a caste dinner.
updates.harilal: About four. Gandhi teaches him and his cousins physical exercise.
updates.ravishankar: Gandhi's Bombay cook, a Brahman who calls the plough his only worship. Gandhi treats him as family and teaches him to cook.
updates.caste: Half the caste readmits Gandhi. He respects the other half's ban without resentment, and they later help his work. He credits this to 'nonresistance'.
updates.ahimsa: Gandhi's quiet acceptance of the caste ban is an early instance of nonresistance working.
updates.diet: Introduces oatmeal and cocoa at home, which end up added to tea and coffee rather than replacing them.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has set up a small household in Bombay to learn Indian law and find work, while family expenses mount at home.
chapters.summary: In his first case, a small claim for Mamibai, Gandhi rises to cross-examine, finds his mind blank, and hands the case to another lawyer. He vows not to appear again until he has the courage. He drafts a petition for a poor Muslim, is turned down as an English teacher for lacking a degree, and closes the Bombay household after six months.

updates.gandhi: Freezes in court in his first case and returns the fee. Refuses to pay touts commission and is rejected for a teaching job. Returns to Rajkot after six months.
updates.mamibai: Gandhi's first client. He collapses during cross-examination and passes her case to Mr. Patel.
updates.virchand: Studies with Gandhi and joins his diet experiments. Tells unnerving stories of barristers who wait years for work.
updates.pherozeshah: His mastery of the Evidence Act is held up as an impossible standard.
updates.law: First case is a fiasco, though his petition-drafting turns out competent. He is too timid for the courtroom.
updates.shyness: Gandhi's shyness ends his first court appearance.
updates.simplicity: Walks 45 minutes each way to the High Court, which keeps him healthy.

chapters.situation: Having failed in Bombay, Gandhi returns to Rajkot to draft petitions through his brother's practice.
chapters.summary: Gandhi earns about Rs. 300 a month drafting applications and compromises his rule against paying commissions to please his brother. His brother is accused of giving bad advice to the Porbandar ruler and asks Gandhi to use an English acquaintance with the British Political Agent. The officer has Gandhi thrown out by his peon. Pherozeshah Mehta advises him to pocket the insult. The shock changes Gandhi's life, and he never again exploits a friendship.

updates.gandhi: Physically thrown out of a British officer's office. Swallows the insult on Pherozeshah's advice and vows never again to trade on a friendship.
updates.laxmidas: Accused of giving wrong advice to the former Ranasaheb of Porbandar. Pressures Mohandas to intercede for him.
updates.politicalagent: Calls Laxmidas an intriguer and has his peon put Gandhi out. Replies that Gandhi was rude.
updates.pherozeshah: Advises Gandhi to tear up his note and 'pocket the insult', since he 'has yet to know life'.
updates.racism: Gandhi's first direct taste of colonial arrogance.
updates.law: Earns about Rs. 300 a month drafting in Rajkot; pays commissions, which he admits was self-deception.

status.gandhi: Petition-writer in Rajkot, humiliated by the Political Agent

chapters.situation: After being humiliated by the Political Agent, Gandhi finds his Rajkot practice blocked, since most of his work would be in that officer's court.
chapters.summary: Gandhi is sickened by the intrigue of Kathiawad's petty states. In Porbandar he wins the Rana some powers but no relief for the overtaxed Mer peasants. A Meman firm, Dada Abdulla & Co., offers him a year in South Africa to help with a £40,000 lawsuit, for a first-class fare and £105. Though it is more a clerk's job than a barrister's, Gandhi accepts at once.

updates.gandhi: Depressed by Kathiawad politics, he accepts a one-year job with Dada Abdulla & Co. in South Africa for £105.
updates.politicalagent: Known for insulting visitors; his hostility blocks Gandhi's practice.
updates.abdulkarim: Offers Gandhi the South Africa job, promising European friends and a light workload.
updates.abdulla: First mentioned: his firm in South Africa has a £40,000 lawsuit underway.
updates.laxmidas: Discusses the South Africa offer with Mohandas; the £105 will help the household.
updates.kathiawad: Gandhi finds the court politics of Kathiawad's small states poisonous.
updates.southafrica: An escape from Kathiawad and a chance to see new places.
updates.law: The South Africa job is barely a barrister's post, more that of the firm's servant.

status.gandhi: Leaving for South Africa on a one-year contract

chapters.situation: Frustrated by Kathiawad, Gandhi has accepted a one-year job with an Indian firm in South Africa and leaves Rajkot.
chapters.summary: Gandhi leaves Kasturbai and a new baby, promising to return in a year. He secures a berth in the chief officer's cabin and sails in April 1893, learning chess from the Captain and nearly being left behind at Lamu. In Zanzibar the Captain takes him to a brothel; Gandhi stands frozen and comes out untouched, his third such escape. He reaches Natal at the end of May.

updates.gandhi: Sails for South Africa in April 1893. Escapes temptation in Zanzibar and arrives in Natal late in May.
updates.kasturba: Has a second baby. Their love is 'getting gradually purer'. Gandhi says goodbye, expecting to be back in a year.
updates.manilal: Born after Gandhi's return from England; Gandhi leaves him as a baby.
updates.captain: Teaches Gandhi chess, holds the ship for him at Lamu, then takes him to a brothel in Zanzibar.
updates.zanzibar: Lamu, Mombasa and Zanzibar: a near miss with the tide and a week of sightseeing.
updates.brahmacharya: Third escape from 'sin', which teaches him to cast off false shame.
updates.natal: Gandhi reaches Natal at the end of May 1893.

chapters.situation: Gandhi has just arrived at Durban to work for Dada Abdulla & Co. on its big lawsuit.
chapters.summary: Abdulla Sheth meets him, unsure what to do with this expensively dressed barrister. In the Durban court the magistrate orders Gandhi to remove his turban; he refuses and walks out. Gandhi learns how Natal's Indians are divided into merchants, clerks and indentured labourers, all called 'coolies'. He defends his turban in the press and is labelled an 'unwelcome visitor'.

updates.gandhi: Refuses to remove his turban in court and writes to the press, getting instant notoriety as the 'coolie barrister'.
updates.abdulla: Doubts the value of the 'white elephant' his brother has sent. Talks with Gandhi about Islam and advises him to keep his turban rather than adopt an English hat.
updates.racism: All Indians are called 'coolies' or 'samis'. The turban rule exempts only Muslim dress.
updates.indians_sa: Gandhi learns how the community is divided, with indentured labourers or girmitiyas the largest group.
updates.islam: Discussions with Abdulla Sheth give Gandhi a practical knowledge of Islam.
updates.natal: Indians are held in little respect at Durban.
